title: Will computers replace doctors?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss whether computers will replace doctors. They cover consumer health-tracking wearables and apps, the bedside manner of diagnostic avatars (including a 2011 World Science Festival kiosk that handled a baby's diarrhea), IBM's Watson and its diagnosis versus treatment roles, the DXplain and Isabel diagnostic programs, the case of diagnostician Dr. Dolly Wall, intuition versus data, misdiagnosis statistics, robotic surgery (da Vinci, fully autonomous surgery, under-reporting of injuries), and smartphone-based self-diagnostic gadgets and proteomics. They conclude humans will still be needed, though computers will assist. The episode ends with a listener mail about weeds and the Scott Fertilizer Company, and an outro with contact information and an ad read.

segments.title: Opening banter and wearable health trackers
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the episode after the holidays and discuss consumer health-tracking devices like Fitbit, Nike Fuelband and Jawbone, plus sites and apps for self-advocacy and informed patients.

segments.title: Will computers replace doctors? Opinions
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the debate over whether physicians will be replaced. Dr. Kent Bottles foresees diagnostic computers replacing GPs, Farhad Manjoo argues specialists are more vulnerable, and Dr. Ashwin (Atul Gawande-style commentary) notes nurses already do the human interface role.

segments.title: Bedside manner and avatars
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether computers can offer good bedside manner, citing a 2011 World Science Festival kiosk avatar that handled a baby's diarrhea and a study finding anxiety patients disclosed more to avatars.

segments.title: Personal care and medical history
segments.summary: They note that personal, longtime family-doctor care has declined and that intimate knowledge of patients' medical histories has been largely lost in modern practice, an area computers could conceivably do better.

segments.title: Diagnostic software history and IBM Watson
segments.summary: The hosts trace diagnostic software from the University of Pittsburgh in the 1970s and Massachusetts General's DXplain system, then describe Watson's strengths with natural language and its potential to combine records, research and tests into ranked diagnoses.

segments.title: Doctors' time limits, Dolly Wall and intuition
segments.summary: They discuss physicians' limited reading time, the habits and forgetting that come with practice, and diagnostician Dr. Dolly Wall, who uses the Isabel program and says it has never offered a diagnosis he missed. The debate of intuition versus data is raised, with the claim that only a portion of physician knowledge is evidence based.

segments.title: Misdiagnosis statistics and the Isabel story
segments.summary: A statistic says one in five US diagnoses are incorrect or incomplete. Johns Hopkins research estimates up to 40,000 ICU deaths yearly from misdiagnosis, with premature closure and anchoring bias cited. The Isabel program was named after the daughter of its creator, whose necrotizing fasciitus was missed after a chicken pox diagnosis.
